title: Economía del agua y su asequibilidad para el derecho de acceso en Puerto Vallarta
rationale: This socio-legal empirical study satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. It examines household/domestic (alongside commercial, industrial, and hotel) access to municipal drinking water and sanitation services in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico (c1), analyzes concrete rule-type legal and tariff mechanisms—connection fees, contracting requirements, increasing-block volumetric tariffs, and eligibility screening rules for domestic tariff subsidies under the municipal utility regulation RPSPAPDATDARMPV and the 2025 Municipal Revenue Law (c2)—and pairs this legal analysis with primary stratified random survey data from 364 D.C.I. users and 100 hotel users (c3, c5) reporting approximate bill tiers, perceived tariff affordability, and perceived supply continuity/security upon bill payment (c4). Although published in Spanish (with an English abstract), full-text translation is directly feasible and the study is eligible under Criterion 10 (c6).

title: Governança das águas na transposição do rio São Francisco em Pernambuco: Uma análise usando o IAD framework de Ostrom
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic — macro water-resource / inter-basin raw-water transfer governance unrelated to household or community water or sanitation service access, per Exclusion Criterion 7). Using Ostrom's IAD framework, interviews (2015–2018), and documentary analysis, the study examines the institutional governance arena of the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF), focusing on federal-state power concentration in SGIB and CBHSF/CNRH, interagency fragmentation, bulk raw-water O&M charges and canal boundary monitoring, and socio-environmental impacts on native Caatinga and indigenous communities. Although it notes in passing that municipal supply systems and secondary reservoirs in the Semiárido are obsolete, it does not examine household or community water/sanitation service access (failing c1), does not analyse a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope (failing narrow c2), and reports institutional/participatory and environmental outcomes rather than service-access outcomes (failing c4). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.

title: Reflejos y sombras de la gestión social del agua para consumo humano en Amubri, Talamanca, Costa Rica (1990-2022)
rationale: This qualitative socio-historical empirical case study (1990-2022) meets all systematic-review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Beyond general water governance, it empirically documents specific legal, administrative, and cost-recovery rules governing Indigenous community drinking-water access and service sustainability in Amubri, Costa Rica: (1) strict tariff-based cost-recovery rules without State subsidy for delegated community aqueducts (ASADAS), flat-tariff and non-metering rules, and inter-community tariff disputes (2,000 vs. 500 colones) driving committee fragmentation; (2) SAGA administrative/financial reporting rules (Category C rating) and lack of legal personality (personería jurídica) under differentiated Indigenous territorial norms, which impede access to public funds, donations, and piping materials; and (3) sanitary orders and chlorination regulations. Full text in Spanish is directly translatable per Criterion 10, and qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for mechanism synthesis.

title: Water and sanitation in Brazil: conflicts, appropriation, and climate injustice; [Água e saneamento no Brasil: conflitos, apropriação e injustiça climática]; [Agua y saneamiento en Brasil: conflictos, apropiación e injusticia climática]

title: Water, rural population and administration techniques: the case of Jequitinhonha Valley, Minas Gerais
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) applying the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. While the qualitative fieldwork (188 rural families in 22 communities in the Jequitinhonha Valley, 1999-2002) describes rural household domestic water scarcity, spring-collection rotation, municipal tanker-truck use, cistern reluctance, and village migration, it does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access. Brazil's Water Law (Law No. 9.433/1997, ANA, river basin committees, bulk water outorga) governs river-basin bulk water resources rather than household service access and is explicitly noted by the authors as having barely influenced local practices in the study period, with river basin committees not yet functioning as spaces of debate or agreement (macro-governance background). Empirically, the study investigates peasant cultural perceptions of natural water quality and informal customary neighbour/kinship sharing of natural springs. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 ('institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), community customary water governance and statutory/municipal governance context would qualify for inclusion.

title: Bem comum e normas costumeiras: a ética das águas em comunidades rurais de Minas Gerais
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic — natural water-resources and rural common-pool moral economy study unrelated to household or community water or sanitation service access, per Exclusion Criterion 7). Based on qualitative fieldwork in 18 rural communities in Minas Gerais, Brazil, the article analyzes peasant cultural conceptions of natural water (springs, streams, rivers) as a divine gift and common good, folk water-quality classifications, and watershed conservation tensions (upstream irrigation diversions, forestry fines restricting wetland farming, and community springhead fencing). It examines no water supply or sanitation service, reports no service-access outcome, and analyzes no legal or administrative rule-type mechanism governing service access (referencing Brazil's Lei das Águas only as unanalysed macro-governance background in the closing section). Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain wording, the study is excluded because it concerns common-pool natural water resource ethics and watershed conservation rather than water or sanitation service access.

title: Institutional capacities for the universalization of access to basic sanitation; [Capacidades institucionais para a universalização do acesso ao saneamento básico]
rationale: This quantitative cross-sectional study of Minas Gerais municipalities (SNIS 2018 and IBGE 2017) satisfies Criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6, and passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 because it examines municipal institutional capacity dimensions (financial, technical, operational, and political/planning capacity). However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): its independent variables capture general municipal resource, staffing, equipment, and planning capacity (per capita revenues/expenditures, presence of municipal technical staff, waste vehicles/workers, and binary existence of a municipal sanitation plan/policy combined into PCA factor scores) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).

title: O desafio do federalismo brasileiro no saneamento básico
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although it cites four illustrative descriptive charts from government databases (SNIS 2017 state-level sewage coverage and municipal management instruments, SIGA Brasil federal agency counts, and SIOP 2015-2019 federal budget execution), it has no empirical methodology, no primary data, no systematic synthesis, and no empirical analysis linking a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism to a household or community service-access outcome. It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading because it addresses macro-governance federalism background rather than a specific rule-type access mechanism, and would likewise be excluded under the plain Criterion 2 wording for lack of empirical evidence.

rationale: This empirical comparative case study evaluates two Mexican municipal drinking-water utilities (2001–2015) using key informant interviews, legal/contractual review, and longitudinal administrative and household-survey indicators. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2 because it directly analyzes utility ownership structure (mixed public-private company vs. paramunicipal utility), tariff and cost-recovery rules (inflation indexation, preferential social tariffs, connection-fee cross-subsidies for low-income households, and unmetered flat-rate discretion), and statutory vs. discretionary/clientelist enforcement of non-payment service disconnections alongside drinking-water coverage, 24/7 service continuity, rationing, and user-reported supply failures. Full text is in Spanish and directly translatable per Criterion 10.

Under the 2026-10-13 adjudication, however, it fails Criterion 2 because it does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/disconnection rules, or analysed ownership/enforcement rules governing access); inactive connections and low coverage are attributed to physical water-source scarcity, deteriorated pumping/pipe infrastructure, generic project delivery deficits, and broad public-works corruption perceptions.

rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. title: The making of Bottom-up Innovations in Urban Water Services in Precarious Neighborhoods of Ouagadougou Case Studies in Goundrin and Boassa; [La fabrique des innovations d’en bas dans les services urbains d’eau des quartiers précaires de Ouagadougou Études de cas à Goundrin et à Boassa]
rationale: Qualitative comparative case study (19 semi-directive interviews plus direct observation in 2022-2023) examining off-grid drinking-water access in two unallotted ('non loti') neighborhoods of Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso. rationale: Include for the systematic review (mechanism synthesis). Full text is in Spanish (with English and Portuguese abstracts) and translation is feasible per Criterion 10.
